scenes.narration: One Tuesday morning, a toaster dies. Its owner, Mel, flips it over and finds three words. Made in China. So she sets out to buy a new one that isn't. The kettle. The lamp. The charger in her pocket. The same three words, again and again.

Since twenty eighteen, the United States has raised tariffs on Chinese goods again and again. Last year, American imports from China fell to about three hundred and nine billion dollars, down from about four hundred and forty billion dollars the year before. And yet China still makes about twenty-seven percent of everything the world manufactures. So why is it so hard to leave?
The answer isn't just cheap labor. Let's walk the factory floor, the street of suppliers, the port, the refinery, and one factory that tried to move away.

Picture a factory floor that makes almost everything. Toasters on one line, phone chargers on the next, then sneakers, batteries and solar panels. That floor is a cartoon, of course. The numbers behind it are not.

Start with size. Manufacturing value added is what factories add on top of the parts and materials they buy. By World Bank data, China's factories added about four point eight trillion dollars in twenty twenty-five. That's about twenty-seven percent of the world total, by our calculation. Back in twenty oh-four, it was about eight and a half percent.

Let me draw that. Here's all the world's factory output in twenty oh-four. China's slice is about one dollar in twelve. Now twenty twenty-five. The whole bar is bigger, and China's slice is more than one dollar in four.

scenes.narration: And it sells that output everywhere. The World Trade Organization says China exported three point seven seven trillion dollars of goods in twenty twenty-five, more than any other country, about fourteen percent of the world total. It sold so much more than it bought that its goods surplus reached one point one nine trillion dollars.

It has the people, too. China's statistics bureau counted about two hundred and thirteen million people working in industry and construction at the end of twenty twenty-four. That count includes builders, not just factory hands. But it gives you the scale.

Are they still cheap? A production worker at a larger Chinese company earned roughly eleven thousand two hundred dollars in twenty twenty-five, at the Federal Reserve's average exchange rate. An American factory production worker earned about twenty-nine dollars an hour. Cheaper, clearly. But Chinese factory pay keeps rising, up about six percent last year at private firms. If wages were the whole story, factories would simply chase the lowest pay on the map. Many of them didn't.

Here's what holds them. Picture a street where every part is a few minutes away. Screws on one corner. Cables on the next. Molds, motors, glass, batteries, circuit boards. An engineer changes a design in the morning and holds a new sample by the afternoon. Economists call this a supplier cluster. It's speed you can't put in a container.

Let me draw why that matters. Box one is the final assembler. Around it, dozens of suppliers. When they're close, a missing part is a phone call and a short ride. Move the assembler far away, and every arrow becomes a container, a customs form and weeks at sea.

The deepest clusters are in the newest industries. The International Energy Agency says China made about seventy percent of the world's electric cars in twenty twenty-five, and more than eighty percent of battery cells. For the chemical powders inside those cells, it's higher still. about eighty-five percent of the cathode powder. more than ninety percent of the anode powder.

The agency calls it a tightly clustered supply chain, from refining minerals to building the car. And it shows up in the price. In twenty twenty-five, battery packs in China were thirty percent cheaper than in North America.

Solar panels tell the same story. In a twenty twenty-two report, the IEA found that China's share of every manufacturing stage, from polysilicon to wafers, cells and modules, was above eighty percent. The ten biggest makers of the machines that make the panels were Chinese. And making panels there cost twenty percent less than in the United States.

Then there's a step most people never see. Rare earth elements go into the magnets inside electric motors and wind turbines. Digging them up is only the start. They have to be separated and refined. For magnet rare earths, the IEA puts China's share of refining at eighty-five percent in twenty twenty-five, down from ninety percent a year earlier. And in April twenty twenty-five, China put export controls on seven of them.

When it's all built, it has to leave. In twenty twenty-five, the port of Shanghai handled fifty-five million containers, counted in twenty-foot units. The port of Los Angeles handled about ten million. That's more than five times as many through one Chinese port, by our calculation.

Add highways, power plants, and a deep bench of tooling engineers, line managers and technicians who have launched products many times, and you get the real advantage. Not one cheap factory. A whole neighborhood that works together, fast.

Washington's answer was tariffs. In twenty eighteen, the U.S. Trade Representative put a twenty-five percent tariff on about thirty-four billion dollars of Chinese goods a year, then on sixteen billion dollars more. In September, a ten percent tariff hit about two hundred billion dollars, raised to twenty-five percent the next spring. Another round followed in twenty nineteen, and part of it was cut in half under a trade deal in early twenty twenty.

In twenty twenty-four, a review raised tariffs on strategic products. one hundred percent on Chinese electric cars. fifty percent on solar cells. And fifty percent on semiconductors from twenty twenty-five.

Then, in twenty twenty-five, new tariffs under an emergency-powers law were stacked on top. In April, the so-called reciprocal tariff on Chinese goods reached one hundred and twenty-five percent, before it was cut back in May. In February twenty twenty-six, the Supreme Court ruled that the law does not authorize tariffs at all. Other laws took over. Since July twenty twenty-six, Chinese goods have faced a twelve and a half percent tariff under one of them.

Remember who pays. A tariff is collected at the border from the American company that imports the goods. Some of it reaches shoppers. Federal Reserve economists estimated that at least thirty percent of the tariff cost on Chinese imports had shown up in retail prices by the end of twenty twenty-five. The rest was absorbed somewhere along the way.

Did it work? Partly. U.S. imports from China peaked at about five hundred and thirty-nine billion dollars in twenty eighteen. In twenty twenty-five, they fell by twenty-nine percent in a single year, to about three hundred and nine billion dollars.

But watch the boxes. In the first nine months of twenty twenty-six, imports from China were down about eleven percent from a year earlier. Month by month, though, they climbed again, from about nineteen billion dollars in February to about thirty-one and a half billion dollars in September.
So many companies tried a different plan. Keep China, and add one more country. Factory people call it China plus one. And America's import data shows where the orders went.

Let me chart America's import shares, from Census data, by our calculation. In twenty seventeen, China supplied about a fifth of U.S. goods imports. In the first nine months of twenty twenty-six, less than eight percent. Vietnam went from two percent to more than seven percent. Taiwan, from under two percent to almost eight percent. Mexico, from thirteen percent to seventeen percent. India grew too, but slowly, to about three percent.

But follow the parts. In twenty twenty-five, China's exports to Southeast Asia rose thirteen percent. The WTO notes that part of that growth is parts and materials for products whose buyers live somewhere else. A new factory can move the final assembly, while many of its parts still come from the old neighborhood.

Moving the deeper layers is slow. A new plant needs suppliers that don't exist there yet, roads and ports that can handle the volume, steady power, and people trained to run the line. Until all of that arrives, the boxes keep coming back.

Still, it is happening. The IEA says the largest share of America's electric car imports in twenty twenty-five came from Mexico. Battery factory capacity grew faster in Europe and the United States than in China. And in Southeast Asia, one-third of electric cars sold came from a Vietnamese carmaker.

The new places face tariffs, too. Since July twenty twenty-six, Vietnam's rate under that same action is twelve and a half percent, the same as China's. Mexico's is ten percent, with exemptions for goods that follow the North American trade agreement.

So why does the world still depend on Chinese factories? Not because of one cheap wage. Because of a neighborhood. Suppliers down the street, refiners for the hidden materials, ports that never sleep, and engineers who have done it before. Tariffs can move the last step. Rebuilding the whole neighborhood takes far longer. That's why, even after years of trade war, more than a quarter of the world's manufacturing still happens in one country. The next factory may well open in Vietnam, Mexico or India. Its parts list is the hard part to move.
